newsitem.title: USA: Huang knowingly broke law for Democrats - Senator.
newsitem.headline: Huang knowingly broke law for Democrats - Senator.

text.p: Former Democratic Party fund-raiser John Huang was at the centre of a scheme to knowingly raise illegal foreign funds for the Democratic Party, the chairman of a Senate investigation said on Thursday.

Tennessee Republican Fred Thompson, who chairs the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee investigating campaign fundraising misdeeds, said Huang "did not raise illegal contributions in 1996 from mistake or lack of knowledge."

The committee had uncovered illegal contributions dating back to 1992 which were "evidence of a common scheme or plan to raise illegal campaign funds," Thompson said at the opening of Thursday's hearing.

Summarizing the results of the first five days of testimony, Thompson said Huang had raised more than $1.6 million, which the Democratic Party had subsequently returned. Most of that money came from foreign interests.

Republicans are trying to show that Huang may have betrayed U.S. secrets to his former Lippo employees, who in turn could have passed them on to China. However, so far they have only presented circumstantial evidence suggesting that this could conceivably have happened.

Huang, an Asian-American, worked at the Commerce Department from June 1994 to January 1996 before becoming a fund-raiser for the Democratic National Committee. He has refused to cooperate with the Senate investigation unless granted some form of immunity from prosecution.
Before joining the Clinton administration, Huang worked for the Lippo Group, a multi-billion dollar conglomerate with mostly Asian interests which has close links with China.
Thompson said Lippo's principal Chinese partner, the government-controlled China Resources, was used by the Beijing government as an "agent of economic and political espionage."
Committee investigator Jack Cobb testified that while at the Commerce Department, Huang had phoned officials or consultants of Lippo hundreds of times.
Cobb also suggested that Huang continued fund raising for the Democrats while working for the government.

Huang received secret briefings about China and visited the Chinese embassy and those of other Asian nations. He had access to classified State Department cables and saw up to 550 raw intelligence reports on China.
He also visited the White House 67 times, several of them for meetings with President Bill Clinton.
Attorney General Janet Reno said the FBI had reviewed Thompson's statement for classified information but his conclusions were his own, not those of law enforcement.

In Hong Kong, China Resources launched a campaign to defend its name on Thursday, saying it was victim of "irresponsible, malicious and slanderous attacks on the company's reputation." It threatened legal action against anyone repeating such allegations.

The committee heard evidence from the secretary of a stockbroking company with offices across the street from the Commerce Department who testified that Huang often used a telephone in the office and received packages.
But the secretary, Paula Greene, knew nothing of the content of the packages and did not know who Huang called.
"These visits to the office I find very curious but I can't conclude anything more from them," Democratic Sen. Joseph Lieberman of Connecticut said after more than an hour of testimony.
